## Lecture 6: Getting Started with Python (Q1 to Q15)

**Q1.** Which statement about Python and Google Colab is correct?

A.  Colab is the language, and Python is the interface where you type it
B.  Python is the language and Colab the interface, and in Colab the Python runs on Google's computers
C.  Colab runs Python on your own laptop, so Python has to be installed on it first
D.  A Colab notebook is saved as a `.py` file in your laptop's Downloads folder

**Q2.** A Colab code cell contains only these four lines. What appears under the cell when it is run?

```{.python}
spend = 24345.78
revenue = 76928.88
revenue / spend
spend
```

A.  Nothing, because the cell has no `print()`
B.  `3.159834...`, the revenue per euro spent
C.  `3.159834...` and `24345.78`, on two lines
D.  `24345.78`

**Q3.** Your Colab runtime is stopped after you leave it idle for too long. You had uploaded `insta-data.csv` and created several variables. What have you lost?

A.  The variables and the uploaded file, but not the code in the cells
B.  The code in the cells, unless the notebook was downloaded first
C.  Nothing, because Colab saves your variables and files to Google Drive
D.  Only the uploaded file, because the variables are stored in the notebook

## Answer key

Each row gives the keyed letter and the reason, which can also serve as the feedback students see after the test.

45 questions on Lectures 6 to 8, each with four options and one correct answer, with the same level mix as Test 1 of BAA1118 (4 easy, 34 medium, 7 hard). Every code question was run in Python (pandas 3, matplotlib 3.11, seaborn 0.13) to confirm its key, and the Loomrow figures were checked against `insta-data.csv`.

| Q | Answer | Topic | Level | Why |
|:--|:---|:--------|:---|:------------------------------|
| 1 | **B** | Language vs interface | Medium | Python is the engine and Colab the dashboard. Colab runs your Python on Google's computers, so nothing is installed on your laptop, and the notebook is a `.ipynb` file in the Colab Notebooks folder of your Google Drive. |
| 2 | **D** | Notebook output | Medium | A code cell displays the value of its last line only, and the last line is `spend`. To see the ratio as well, wrap it in `print()`. |
| 3 | **A** | The runtime | Medium | Everything you create lives in the runtime: variables, tables and uploaded files. Your code is safe in the notebook; your results and uploads are not. Upload the file again and rerun from the top. |
| 4 | **B** | Cells run in the order you run them | Hard | Colab runs cells in the order you click them, not top to bottom. Cell 2 ran twice, adding 1,000 each time: 5,000, then 6,000, then 7,000. **Runtime** → **Restart session and run all** would give 6,000. |
| 5 | **C** | Comments | Medium | Everything after `#` is ignored, whole lines and ends of lines. Only `spend = 50` and `spend = spend + 10` run. |
| 6 | **A** | Storing a result | Medium | `roas` was computed once, when its line ran: 600 / 200. Changing `revenue` afterwards does not update it. `/` always gives a decimal, so it prints `3.0`, not `3`. |
| 7 | **D** | round() | Medium | `round(value, digits)` rounds to that many decimals; without the second value it rounds to a whole number. |
| 8 | **C** | Naming rules | Easy | A name cannot start with a digit: `spend_2025` works, `2025_spend` fails. Letters, digits and underscores are all allowed elsewhere. |
| 9 | **B** | Types | Easy | Between quotes, a number is text, a `str`. `float("24345.78")` would make it a decimal. |
| 10 | **B** | Type decides what works | Medium | `+` joins two strings, `"2"` and `"3"` give `"23"`, and adds two numbers. Same operator, different types, different behaviour. |
| 11 | **C** | Converting text to a number | Medium | `int()` turns the text into a whole number, which can then be compared: 535,086 is more than 518,400. Text compared with a number, or text plus a number, is a `TypeError`; `int("reach_text")` tries to convert the word itself, a `ValueError`. |
| 12 | **D** | Comparisons | Medium | Text comparison is case sensitive, so `"Reel" == "reel"` is `False`. `!=` means not equal, and `"Reel"` is not `"image"`. |
| 13 | **A** | Error types | Medium | The quote is never closed, so Python cannot read the line: a `SyntaxError`. `Reach` never created is a `NameError`; text times text and text plus a number are `TypeError`s. |
| 14 | **D** | Reading errors | Hard | Python stops at line 3, the first line that fails: it is case sensitive, so `reach` does not exist, only `Reach`. Fixing it would reveal the `TypeError` on line 4, then the `Print` on line 5. |
| 15 | **A** | Fixing an error | Medium | Commas inside `print()` display several values of any type, with a space between them. `int(431)` is still a number; option C still adds text and a number; `Print` is not `print`. |
| 16 | **C** | Importing pandas | Medium | A restart empties the runtime, so `pd` exists only once the first cell has run again. pandas is installed in Colab already; a missing file gives a `FileNotFoundError`, and a misspelt `panda` a `ModuleNotFoundError`. |
| 17 | **D** | Reading a CSV file | Easy | The file name goes between quotes, spelt exactly as in the Files panel, extension included. Colab runs on Linux, where `Insta-data.csv` is another file. |
| 18 | **A** | Attributes vs methods | Medium | `.shape` is a value the table has, so no brackets: with them, `TypeError: 'tuple' object is not callable`. `insta.info` without brackets shows `<bound method ...>`, and `.size` is also a value, not a method. |
| 19 | **B** | Missing values | Medium | `object` means text (newer versions of pandas write `str`), and Non-Null Count is the number of values present: 431 - 206 = 225 posts went out outside any campaign. Missing does not mean wrong: find out what it means before you drop or fill it. |
| 20 | **C** | describe(): mean vs median | Medium | Half of the posts reach less than the median, 5,184. A few huge posts, starting with LR0184 and its 535,086 accounts, pull the mean up to almost twice the median. |
| 21 | **B** | Selecting columns | Medium | The inner brackets are a list of names; the outer brackets select. One name in one pair of brackets gives a Series; a list gives a DataFrame. |
| 22 | **B** | rename() returns a new table | Medium | `rename()` returns a renamed copy, and nothing stored it. `posts = posts.rename(...)` would keep it. |
| 23 | **D** | & and \| | Medium | `&` keeps the rows where both conditions are true: the two reels above 50,000. `|` keeps those where either is: the three reels, plus the image at 75,000. |
| 24 | **A** | Writing two conditions | Medium | Each condition needs its own round brackets, joined by `&`. Without brackets, Python reads `"reel" & insta["reach"]` first and fails; `and` does not work on columns (`ValueError`); one `=` is a `SyntaxError`. |
| 25 | **C** | isin() and between() | Hard | `isin()` keeps the two Denim posts and the Knitwear one. `between(1000, 2000)` includes both ends, so 1,000, 2,000 and 1,999 are kept. |
| 26 | **B** | Booleans are not text | Hard | `True` is a value, like a number, and takes no quotes. No cell holds the text `"True"`, so no row matches: the filter returns an empty table, without an error. |
| 27 | **A** | Sorting rows | Medium | `ascending=False` puts the largest reach first, LR02 with 61,000. A sort makes a copy: `posts` keeps its order unless the result is stored back in it. |
| 28 | **C** | Creating a column | Medium | The new name on the left adds a fourth column, and the formula runs on every row: 360 / 6,000 × 100 = 6.0 and 100 / 2,000 × 100 = 5.0. The number of rows does not change. |
| 29 | **D** | groupby() | Medium | The reels reached 5,200, 61,000 and 1,500: their median is 5,200. 67,700 is their sum and 22,566.7 their mean, pulled up by the 61,000. |
| 30 | **A** | pivot_table() | Hard | There is no paid image, so the combination has nothing to count, and pandas marks the cell as missing, `NaN`. `count` counts values of any type, text included. |
| 31 | **D** | Why plot the data | Easy | Anscombe's four datasets share their means, standard deviations, correlation and best-fit line, yet look nothing alike. Only the charts tell them apart. |
| 32 | **A** | The canvas: fig and ax | Medium | `plt.subplots()` gives back two things: `fig`, the whole figure, and `ax`, its plotting area. Every layer is a method of `ax`; `plt.show()` comes last, to display the result. |
| 33 | **B** | Mapping x and y | Medium | A geometry's first argument is the x column, across; the second is the y column, up. |
| 34 | **C** | Choosing a geometry | Medium | A histogram cuts one column into bins and counts the posts in each: the distribution. `ax.histogram` does not exist (`AttributeError`), `ax.plot()` would join the rates in the table's order, and `ax.bar()` needs heights as well as positions. |
| 35 | **C** | Line charts | Medium | A line joins the rows in the order of the table, not of the x values. Sort first: `by_date = insta.sort_values("posted_at")`. |
| 36 | **B** | Bar charts from value_counts() | Medium | `value_counts()` gives one count per format, with the formats as its index: `counts.index` for the positions on x, `counts.values` for the heights. Swapped, the code runs but the chart is meaningless; `ax.bar()` without heights is a `TypeError`, and `ax.hist(counts)` counts the counts. |
